*51.    DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA:†                         
SHRI LALIT KISHORE CHATURVEDI: 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased 
to state: 
(a) what is the total shortage of teachers in Prima ry to Higher Secondary, 
Group-wise, in Government Schools in India as a who le, State-wise, and 
Rajasthan in particular as on date; 
(b) whether the National Institute of Educational P lanning and 
Administration has submitted any report in this context;

of teachers in schools;

(f) what is teacher-student ratio at present and how does it compare with the 
idea! ratio?

Drop-out rate of girl students 
*63. SHRI RAJEEV SHUKLA: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that number of girl students w ho drop out of 
schools at all levels is uniformly and significantl y higher than that of boy 
students; 
(b) whether Government have any scheme underway that seeks to rectify this 
anomaly; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ARJUN SINGH): (a) to (d) A statement is laid on the Table of the Sabha. 
(a) In 2003-04, the drop-out rates for girl students in the country as a whole 
at the primary stage (Classes l-V), at elementary s tage (Classes I-VIII) and 
secondary stage (Classes l-X) were 28.6%, 52.9% and 64.9% respectively. At 
the primary stage, the drop-out rate for girls was lower than that of boys, 
whereas for elementary and secondan/stages, they we re higher than that of 
boys. 
(b) to (d) Under Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, a multi-pronged approach has been 
adopted for reducing drop-out rates. One set of int erventions relates to 
strengthening of primary and upper primary schools and improving the 
9 

RAJYA SABHA [27 November, 2006] 
quality of education through improvement in school infrastructure, 
recruitment of additional teachers, annual school g rants, regular training of 
teachers, introduction of good and innovative teach ing practices that make 
class rooms more joyful and attractive regular academic support to teachers, etc. 
On the other hand, several interventions aim at imp roving the demand for 
schooling through community mobilization, special i nterventions for 
enrolment and retention of vulnerable groups of chi ldren including girls and 
children of weaker sections. Measures are also bein g undertaken to strengthen 
the accountability of the school system towards parents and the community. The 
Mid-Day Meal Scheme that provides a cooked meal to all children of 
Government and Government-aided primary schools, Ed ucation Guarantee 
Scheme (EGS) Centres and Alternative and Innovative Education (AIE) centers, 
also has the potential for promoting school enrolment and participation. 
Free textbooks are provided to all girls and all SC and ST students up to the 
elementary stage. Under the National Programme for Education of Girls of the 
Elementary Level (NPEGEL), additional resources are  provided to 3164 
educationally backward blocks for interventions of community mobilization, 
bridge courses for out-of school girls, stregthenin g of model cluster schools, 
gender sensitization of teachers etc. to promote retention of girls in primary and 
upper primary schools. 1000 Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalayas (KGBV) which 
are residential schools for girls at upper primary level, particularly for girls from 
disadvantaged sections of society, have been approved in the current year besides 
1180 KGBVs sanctioned earlier in educationally back ward blocks of the 
country. 
As per a new Scholarship scheme introduced by Centr al Board of 
Secondary Education (CBSE) from the academic session 2006-07, a girl who is 
the only child of her parents and who secures 60% o r more marks in class X 
examination for the year 2006 onwards under CBSE system, would be given a 
scholarship of Rs. 500 per month for studying in classes XI and XII in a CBSE 
affiliated school which charges tution fee of not more than Rs. 1000 per month. 
All Kendirya Vidayalayas provide fee waiver to sing le girl children from 
classes VI to XII. 
In Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalayas, one third of the se ats are reserved for 
girls.

SHRI RAJEEV SHUKLA: Sir, the Hon. Minister has given a long reply in 
which it has been mentioned that the drop out rate has gone up to 63 per cent, 
which is very alarming. Despite all the provisions in the scheme, I want to know 
from the Hon. Minister why the drop out rate is inc reasing in the case of girl 
students. 
SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI: Sir, the reasons for drop out rate vary. 
They could be socio-economic; they could also be sc hool-related problems. 
When we look at the socio-economic reasons, these could be girl children, who 
are required to work in their households, their own businesses, their' own farms 
and also could be asked to work outside for remuneration. When we look at the 
school-related factors, it could be accessibility o f schools and it could also be 
the teacher problems that we have been just discussing about. But, Sir, measures 
have been taken to ensure that the schools are brought into close accessibility of 
the children. Under the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, we have ensured that schools are 
opened in each and every habitation. And, wherever there are no schools, we have 
ensured that EGS Centres and AIE Centres are also being opened. Besides this, we 
have also ensured, at least, we have framed the gui delines to such an extent 
that the 50 per cent of the teachers enrolled shoul d be women so that the girls 
could be encouraged to come to school. 
SHRI RAJEEV SHUKLA: Yes, this is a major problem, S ir. Most of the 
parents are reluctant to send their girl children to the schools where only male 
teachers are available. Is there any special scheme the Government is envisaging 
to recruit more and more female teachers? 
SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI: Sir, as I have already me ntioned 
earlier, the guidelines clearly say that the 50 per  cent of the teachers enrolled, 
especially in the primary schools, should be woman teachers. So, it is up to the 
States to ensure that they enrol 50 per cent women teachers.. 
SHRI RAJEEV SHUKLA: But, what is the status? Fifty per cent woman 
teachers are not there. Are you doing something to enforce this? 
SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI: Whenever such things are brought to 
our notice, we do take it up with the concerned State Governments.

creation of infrastructure. Even in infrastructure, provision of toilets has been 
awarded very high priority. Today, in about 34 to 3 5 per cent of schools, we

very closely linked to the absence of the right to education as a fundamental right 
which was assured by this UPA Govemment in its Common Minimum Programme,

recall that in the last session of Parliament I had raised this issue and there was 
no reply forthcoming — my question to the Minister is: When the CABE has 
recommended the right to education legislation and the UPA Government's 
Common Minimum Programme has assured the right to education legislation, what 
is keeping the Government back? And why has the Government withdrawn its 
responsibility for this and put it on the States? This is the issue, because that is 
the only way, Sir, in which girl drop-outs can be stopped.

girls, who come from backward and poor families, to  complete their 
education, especially in the rural areas, we have s tarted Kanya Vidya Dhan 
Scheme under which Rs. 20,000 are given to every gi rl, cutting across the 
religious and caste lines, whenever she completes intermediate. This Scheme has 
helped a lot in stopping this drop-out rate of girls. I want to know whether the 
Central Government has learned anything from this Scheme. Are they going to 
implement this Scheme at a broader level across the country? 
SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI: Sir, various States have implemented 
programmes giving good initiative to ensure that girl children go to school. Uttar 
Pradesh, for example, has launched its Meena Manch.  Haryana has provided 
bicycles to girl children who are studying in Class-VI. Similarly, Orissa has the 
Kalasi Dhara Scheme launched. Bihar has the Summer Camp which actually 
conduct remedial classes. Puducherry also has a goo d intervention for girl 
education. But other than this, Sir, I think if the State Governments could come 
out with innovative schemes like this to ensure tha t the girl children come to 
school, this would be very encouraging. Besides thi s, even in the secondary 
level of education also, under the CBSE Scheme, various initiatives have been 
launched by the

in the name of the girl child studying in Class IX and this money could be

Scheme for girl education 
*62. SHRI TARIQ ANWAR: Will the Minister of HUMAN R ESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have prepared any special scheme/project for girl 
education in the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the names of the districts which are covered under this scheme, 
especially in Bihar and Maharashtra? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ARJUN SINGH): (a) tojc) At the elementary stage of education, the Sarva 
Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA), the National Programme for E ducation of Girls at 
Elementary Level (NPEGEL) and the Kasturba Gandhi B alika Vidyalaya 
(KGBV) programmes are the principal programmes to address girls education. 
The SSA covers all districts of the country while t he NPEGEL and KGBV 
programmes are focused on Educationally Backward Bl ocks (EBBs) in the 
country. All eligible EBBs in Bihar and Maharashtra have been covered under 
the NPEGEL programme and 128 EBBs in Bihar and 27 i n Maharashtra, 
under the KGBV scheme. 
At the higher secondary level, the Central Board of  Secondary Education 
(CBSE) has a scholarship scheme for the meritorious  single girl child 
studying in schools affiliated to it.

Development of National Disaster Information System 
*64. SHRI VEDPRAKASH P. GOYAL: Will the Minister of  SCIENCE 
AND TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Govemment are planning to  develop a National 
Disaster Information System (NDIS), which will aler t all citizens before any 
natural disaster and terrorist attack through their  mobile phones, landlines 
and wireless; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) how long it will take to be functional; and 
(d) how far it will be useful in protecting us in'the event of any disaster? 
THE MINISTER OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY AND MINISTER  
OF EARTH SCIENCES (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) and (b) Technologies are 
being developed which will allow us in the future t o alert citizen before the 
natural disaster. The nature of the technology will  differ depending upon the 
nature of the disaster. Pilot projects are being un dertaken to develop such 
technologies and to acquire capabilities for alerti ng our citizens. Thus far, we 
do not have the necessary technology in place. 
In case of Natural Disasters which are results of Cyclones, Typhoons, Storm 
surges, Tsunami, etc. it is possible to give advance information. By monitoring 
such natural events it is technologically possible to alert our citizens in advance 
because of the time lead involved in such natural events reaching and impacting 
our citizens. But natural disasters such as earthqu akes, cloud burst, etc. with 
the technology available thus far, are difficult to predict. Science is in the process 
of better understanding such phenomenon with the hope of developing technologies 
for providing possible alerts in future. 
Technology Development Board (TDB), Department of S cience and 
Technology, has provided financial assistance to a company M/s Geneva Software 
Technologies Limited, Bangalore for a pilot project for development of Natural 
Disaster Information System (NDIS) under which alert messages generated in 
English language at IMD were converted automatically in regional languages 
and sent under text / voice mode to the identified telephone/mobile numbers, 
and also in voice mode through wireless, in the selected areas of Nagapattinam 
coastal area and at Chennai city. 
17 

RAJYA SABHA [27 November, 2006] 
As far as terrorist attacks are concered, it is difficult to alert the citizens based on 
the available technologies. However, it is possible to envisage the development of 
appropriate technologies in the future depending upon the nature of terrorist attacks. 
(c) and (d) Pilot project has been technically developed and successfully demonstrated. 
However, in order to make it f unctbnal, we require resources andnetwork for the same. It is 
difficult to say when such a system will be fully functional. 
It may be mentioned that the technology developed i s a generic technology 
and it has got multiple applications in information system for alerting and also 
giving messages of social relevance. Such technolog y can also be used for 
disseminating/sending audio messages to land line phones and also disseminating 
information through the wireless public address systems. Such information can be 
disseminated in case of rains, floods, landslides, railway accidents, traffic jams, health 
related messages, fires, etc. 
In order to transmit the messages pertaining to naturai disasters etc. there is 
need to develop/provide public private partnership for effective communication. 
The message can also be transmitted as scrolling message on T.V. networks. 
The technology has been demonstrated to the Ministry of Home Affairs and 
National Disaster Management Authority for further appropriate action. 
Speedy disposal of criminal cases 
*65.  SHRIMATI MOHSINA KIDWAI: 
SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: 
Will the Minister of LAW AND JUSTICE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have studied the recent observations of the Supreme 
Court of India that around 1.77 crore criminal cases are pending in various courts 
across the country and that "Government must take necessary steps immediately to 
enforce the right to speedy trial of an accused" which is one of the facets of the 
fundamental right to life and liberty enshrined in Article 21 of the Constitution; 
(b) if so, the results thereof; and 
18 

[27 November, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) the details of steps initiated to liquidate thi s huge backlog and also for 
speedy trial of cases to make the administration of  criminal justice effective, 
vibrant and meaningful? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ ): 
(a) to (c) Government is aware of the size of pende ncy of criminal cases in 
various courts across the country, and has, from ti me to time taken steps to 
reduce the backlog of cases and facilitate faster'trial by courts, at the same time 
ensuring the observance of the provisions of article 21 of the Constitution. 
With a view to liquidating cases pending for long i n the Sessions Courts 
Government introduced a scheme of Fast Track Courts which has been extended 
upto 31.3.2010. Government reviews the Judge strength (in High Courts) triennially 
and ensures prompt filling up of vacancies so that justice administration does not 
suffer from inadequate number of judges. In respect of filling up of vacancies in the 
Subordinate Courts, a matter falling within the dom ain of the State 
Governments, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has given directions to the States in 
the Malik Mazhar Sultan case. State Governments have been reminded in this 
regard from time to time. 
Government has, with a view to ensuring speedy disp osal of cases, made 
appropriate changes in the Code of Criminal Procedu re through Code of 
Criminal Procedure (Amendment) Act, 2005, which inter alia, introduces the 
concept of 'plea bargaining'.

*70 SHRI PRASANTA CHATTERJEE: Will the Minister of WOMEN 
AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the incidents of violence on domestic helpers are on rise in recent 
times; 
(b) whether Government will agree to conduct a nation w ide survey on 
conditions of minors engaged as domestic helpers; and 
(c) the actions being taken for rehabilitation of minor s working as 
domestic helpers? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) to (c)  
Government has recently issued a Notification prohi biting employment of 
children in the following two Occupations with effect from 10.10.06. 
(i)   Employment of children as domestic workers/servants 
(ii) Employment of children in dhabas-(roadside eat eries), restaurants, 
hotels, motels, tea-shops, spas and other recreational centres etc. 
These two occupations have been prohibited on the recommendations of the 
Technical Advisory Committee constituted under the Child Labour (Prohibition 
and Regulation) Act, 1986 which is headed by the Di rector General, Indian 
Council for Medical Research and has various other experts like Director, National 
Institute of Occupational Health, Director General,  Factory Advice Services 
Labour Institute^ Mumbai, Head of Paediatrics Department, AIIMS, Additional 
Director General, Health Services etc. 
Government is implementing the National Child Labou r Project (NCLP) 
Scheme in 250 districts of 20 States in the country. Under the Scheme, there is 
provision for conducting child labour survey in the districts where NCLP scheme 
is under implementation. Another, 21 districts have  been taken up under the 
INDUS project, an Indo-US Child Labour Project. Gov ernment is 
contemplating to conduct a survey in all districts of the country during the 
Eleventh Plan Period on the number of children working' in hazardous occupations 
and processes including domestic child labour. 
Under the NCLP Scheme, children withdrawn from work  are provided 
education, nutrition, vocational training, stipend and helath care etc. In

Meteorological informations to farmers 
t401. SHRI MANGANI LAL MANDAL: Will the Minister of  EARTH 
SCIENCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Meteorological Depart ment has not yet 
attained the capability of making available the met eorological information 
relevant for farmers to all regions and agro-climatic conditions on time; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the Agri-metro Commi ssion of World 
Meteorological Organisation his impressed upon impl ementing new 
technolgies in order to make available meteorologic al information to all the 
farmers of the world, including India on time; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof and the action taken by Government in this regard?

It is a fact that the India Meteorological Departme nt (IMD) has not yet 
attained the capability of making available the kin d of meteorological 
information which our farmers are looking for in re spect of their requirements 
while cultivating their land. The information avail able thus far is neither 
district specific nor field specific. The Commissio n of Agricultural 
Meteorological (CAgM) of World Meteorological Organ isation (WMO) has 
recommended strengthening of agrometeorology services and use of advanced 
information technology to address agricultural haza rds and early warning. 
However, the IMD is able in the short term to disse minate information to our 
farmers in respect of regional agro-climatic condit ions. Such information, 
however, is not the kind of information that needs to be disseminated to the 
farmers for helping them in their agricultural acti vities. However, steps are

more accurate and area specific agro-climate inform ation for dissemination at

manpower. The Ministry is taking appropriate steps to provide such 
infomration to our farmers.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI): (a) to (e) The Report of 
the J.M. Lyngdoh Committee has been submitted to Supreme Court of India and

Statement  
The recommendations of the Committee accepted by Hon'ble Supreme Court 
for implementation are as under:  
1. Conduct of Elections 
1.1 Universities and colleges across tne country must ordinarily conduct 
elections for the appointment of students to student representative bodies These 
elections may be conducted m the manner prescribed herein, or in a manner that 
conforms to the standards prescribed herein. 
1.2 Where the atmosphere of the university campus is adverse to the conduct 
ofpeaceful, free and fair elections, the university , its constituent colleges and 
departments must initiate a system of student representation based on nominations, 
especially where elections are being hold at presen t. It would be advisable, 
however, not to base such nomination system on pure ly academic merit as is 
being practiced throughout the country. 
1.3 In.cases whete elections are not being held, or where the nomination model 
prevails, the nomination model should be allowed to continue for a limited period 
of time. It is to be noted that the nomination system suffers from several flaws, and 
must only be restored to as an INTERIM MEASURE. 
1.4 Subject to the recommendations in respect of the po ssible model of 
elections, all institutions must over a period of 5 years, convert from the 
75 

RAJYASABHA [27November, 2008] 
nomination model to a structured election model, that may be based on system 
of parliamentary (Indirect) elections or on the presidential (direct) system, or a 
hybrid of both, It is highly desirable that all institution follow this mechanism of 
gradual conversion, especially for privately funded  institutions that prefer a 
status quo situation. 
1.5 All institutions must conduct a review of the stude nt representation 
mechanism. The first review may be conducted after a period of 2 years of the 
implementation of the mechanism details above, and the second review may be 
conducted after the 3rd or the 4th year of implemen tation. The primary 
objective of these reviews will be to ascertain the success of the representation 
and election mechanism in each individual institution, so as to decide whether or 
not to implement a full- fledged election structure. Needless to say these reviews 
will be based on a consideration of the views and s uggestions of all 
stakeholders, such as students, faculty, administra tion, student bodies, and 
parents. 
1.6 Institutions must, as a primary objective, subject to the pertinent issue 
of discipline on campus, seek to implement a struct ured system of student 
elections by conclusion of a period of 5 years from the date of the implemenation 
of the recommendations. 
1.7 Subject to the autonoy of the Unversities in respect of the choice of the 
mode of election, ail universities must institute a n apex student representative 
body that represents ali students, colleges, and departments coming under the 
particular university, tn the event thai the univer sity is geographically 
widespread, individual colleges may constitute their own representative bodies, 
which would further elect representatives for the apex universities body. 
1.8 The union/representative body so elected shall only comprise of regular 
students on the rolls of the institution. No faculty member, nor any member of the 
administration shall be permitted to hold any post on the executive of such 
representative body, nor shall be allowed to be a m ember of any such 
representative body. 
2. Modes of Elections 
2.1 A system of direct election of the office beare rs of the student body, 
whereby all students of all constituent colleges as  well as all students of 
university departments vote directly for the office bearers This model may

JNU/University of Hyderabad), 3nd with a relatively  smaller student 
population. 
in respect of universities will large, widespread campuses and large student 
bodies either of the following models may be adopted. 
2.2 A system of elections, where colleges and campuses directly elect college 
and campus office bearers, as well as unviersity representatives. The university 
representatives form an electoral college, which shall elect the university student 
union office bearers. 
2.3 A system of elections where on one hand, directly e lected college and 
campus office bearers, as well as university repres entatives. The university 
representative form an electoral college, which sha ll eiect the university 
students union office bearers. 
2.4 A system of elections where on orse hand, directly elected class 
representative elect the office bearers of the coll ege, as well as the university 
representatives, and the campus itself directly elects the campus office bearers 
and the university representatives. The university representatives shai! form an 
electoral college, which shall elect the office bea rer of the university aiudent 
union. 
2.5 A system of election wherein class representatives shall be directly 
elected in the colleges and universities campus and  they in turn shall elect the 
office bearers for the college unions and the university campus union. Also they 
shall elect their representatives for university st udent union. These elected 
representative from colleges and university campus shall form the electroal 
college, which shall elect the office bearers of the university student union. This 
model shall be applicable to large university with large number of affiliated 
colleges. 
3, Disassociation of Student Elections and Student Representation from  
Political Parties 
3.1 During the period of the elections no person, who is not a student on the 
rolls of the college/university, shall be permitted  to take part in the election 
process in any capacity. Any person, candidate, or member of the student 
organisation, violating this rule shall be subject to disciplinary proceedings, in 
addition to the candidature, as the case may be being revoked.

4. Frequency and Duration of Election Process 
4.11t is recommended that the entire process of elections, commencing from 
the date of filing of nomination papers to the date  of declaration of results, 
including the campaign period, should not exceed 10 days. 
4.2 It is further recommended that elections be held on a yearly basis and that 
the same should be held between 6 to 8 weeks from the date of commencement 
of the academic session. 
5. Eligiblity Criteria for Candidates 
5.1 U nder graduate students between the ages of 17 and 22 may contest elections. 
This age range may be appropriately relaxed in the case of professional 
colleges, where courses often range between 4 to 5 years. 
5.2 For Post Graduate Students the maximum age limit to legitimately 
contest and election would be 24-25 years. 
5.3 For research Students the maximum age limit to legitimately contest 
an election would foe 28 years. 
5 4 Although the Committee would refrain from presc ribing any particular 
minimum marks to be attained by candidate, the cand idate should in no event 
have any academic arrears in the year of contesting the election. 
5.5 The candidate should have attained the minimum perc entage of 
attendance as prescribed by the university or 75% a ttendance, whichever is 
higher. 
5.6 The candidate shall have one opportunity to contest for the post of office 
bearer, and two opportunities to contest for the post of an executive member. 
5.7 The candidate shall not have a previous criminal record, that is to say he 
should not have been tried and/or convicted of any criminal offence or 
misderrraanor. The candidate shall also not have be en subject to any 
disciplinary action by the University authorities. 
5.8 The candidate must be a regular, full time student of the college/ 
university and should not be a distance/proximate education student. That is to say 
that all eligible candidates must be enrolled in a full time course, the course 
duration being at least one year.

     6. Election - Retated Expenditure and Financial Accountability 
6.1 The maximum permited expenditure per candidate shall be Rs. 5000/-. 
6.2 Each candidate shall within two weeks of the de claration of the 
result, submit complete and certified accounts (to be certified by the 
candidate) to the college/university authorities. T he college/university shall 
publish such audited accounts within 2 days of subm ission of such

funds from any other sources than voluntary contrib utions from the student 
body 
7. Cods of Conduct for Candidates and Elections Adm inistrators 
7.1 No candidate shall indulge in, nor shall abet, any activity, which may 
aggravate existing differences or create mutual haired or cause tension between 
different sastes and communities religious or linguistic, or between any group(s) of 
students. 
7.2 Criticism of other candidates, when made, shall be confined to their 
policies and programs, past record and work. Candid ates shall refrain from 
criticism of all aspects of private life not connected with the public activities of 
the other candidates or supporters of such other candidates. Criticism of other 
candidates, or their supporters based on unverified  allegations or distortion 
shall be avoided. 
7.3 There shall be no appeal to caste or communai f eelings for securing 
votes Piaces of worship, within or without the camp us shall not be used 
for election propaganda. 
7.4 Ali candidates shall be prohibited from indulgi ng or abetting, all 
activities which are considered I D be "corrupt practices' and offences, such as 
bribing of voters, intimidation of voters, impersonation of voters canvassing or 
the use of propaganda within 100 meters of polling stations, holding public 
meetings during the period of 24 hours ending with the hour

7.5 No candidate shall be permitted to make use of printed posters, printed

Candidates may only utilize hand-made posters for the purpose of canvassing,

7.9 During the election period the candidates may hold processions and/or

Electrification of Villages in Rajasthan 
494.      DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA: 
SHRI LALIT KISHORE CHATURVEDI: 
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) the progress of electrification of villages under the Rajiv Gandhi Grameen 
Vidyutikaran Yojana in Rajasthan and what set back/damage has been caused by 
flood havoc in Rajasthan; 
(b) whether all the villages in the State will be lighted up by 2009, the year fixed by 
the Centre for covering all the villages in the country under electrification; and 
(c) if so the details thereof and the present status thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHILKUMAR SHINDE): (a) Rajasthan 
Government has reported electrification of 466 unelectrifted villages and release of 3669 
rural household connections, including 1186 Below Poverty Line (BPL) households 
under Rajiv Gandhi Grameen Vidyutikaran Yojana (RGGVY) as on 17th November, 2006. 
Recent floods in August, 2006, in parts of Rajasthan has reportedly not caused any 
damage to the works except that it has delayed execution of works under RGGVY by 
nearly six weeks. 
(b) All the un-electrified villages in the country including in Rajasthan are envisaged 
to be electrified under RGGVY by 2009. RGGVY integrates actions to be taken by 
Government of India, State Governments, Power Utilities and implementing agencies so 
as to attain the national goal of creation of electricity infrastructure in the rural areas 
for households electrification by 2009. 
(c) Rajasthan Government has so far submitted 41 Detailed Project Reports (DPRs) 
covering electrification of 822 unelectrifted villages, re-electrification of 3655 de-
electrified villages and intensive electrification of 34842 already electrified villages in 32 
districts of the State under RGGVY, involving an outlay of Rs. 1033.25 crore. 27 DPRs 
covering electrification of 734 un-electrified villages, re-electrification of 1040 de-electrified 
villages and intensive electrification of 16237 already electrified villages in 26 districts 
of Rajasthan, involving an outlay of Rs. 480.92 crore have since

Revamp of electricity distribution system 
495. SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have decided to revamp the elect ricity distribution 
system, under which the city Transco would manage the load and maintain transformers, 
Discoms would provide the supply from the pole and the consumer would be able to 
choose his Discom; and 
(b) if so, the details of the new system and how far it would end up in giving relief to 
the consumer against exploitation and over billing? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHILKUMAR SHINDE): (a) and (b) As per 
provisions of the Electricity Act, 2003, a transmission licensee is required to build, 
maintain and operate an efficient, co-ordinated and economical inter-State transmission 
system or intra-state transmission system, as the case may be, and to provide non-
discriminatory open access to its transmission system. 
Underthe Act, a transmission licensee has been debarred from engaging in the business 
of trading of electricity. 
Supply of electricity to consumers is the function of the distribution licensee who is, 
in his area of license, duty bound to supply electricity to all consumers who apply for the 
same. The Act also provides for phased introduction of open access in distribution by the State 
Electricity Regulatory Commssions (SERCs). It provides that the SERC .shall, not later 
than. 27th January, 2009, by regulations, provide such open access to all consumers 
who require a supply of elctricity where the maximum power to be made available at any 
time exceeds one megawatt. These consumers would have the option to choose his supplier 
other than the distribution licensee of his area. 
The Tariff Policy  notified by  Central Govemment provides that in whichever states the 
situation so permits, the Regulatory Commissions should introduce open access even 
prior to this deadline. The policy also lays down the methodology for computation of 
cross subsidy surcharge. 
173 

RAJYASABHA [27 November, 2006] 
As per available information, the SERCs of 19 State s have issued open 
access regulations in distribution and 15 SERCs have also specified the method of 
open access surcharge. So far, 17 applications for grant of open access have 
been approved by the respective SERC in 6 States. 
The Electricity Act also provides for grant of lice nse by the Appropriate 
Commission to two or more persons for distribution of electricity through their 
own distribution system within the same area, subje ct to the compliance with 
the additional requirements relating to the capital  adequacy, credit-worthiness, 
or code of conduct prescribed by the Central Government. Central Government 
has already notified the additional requirements in this regard. 
Under the Act, the distribution licensee is required to establish a forum for 
redressal of grievances of the consumers. Any consu mer, who is aggrieved by 
non-redressal of his grievances may make a representation for representation for 
redressal to an authority known as Ombudsman.

fault zone, where in 1991 earthquake of 6.8 had occurred and its epicenter was

THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHILKUMAR SHINDE): (a) Yes,

(b) Two units of 250 MW each of Tehri Dam & HPP Stagerl (1000 MW) have

Himalayan Geology for determining the safe height o f Tehri Dam, before 
according approval to the implementation of the Teh ri Dam and Hydro-
electric Power Project (1000 MW) in March, 1994.

Billing of electricity consumption 
508. SHRIMATI S. G. INDIRA: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the power utilities resor t to billing their 
consumers on the basis of average consumption on the basis of new norms; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the consumers have been demanding to charge 
on the basis of actual consumption; and 
(c) if so, whether Government have asked the power utilities to consider their 
demand? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHILKUMAR SHINDE): (a) to (c) 
Under the provisions of the Electricity Act, 2003, distribution of electricity is a 
licensed activity and is regulated by the State Ele ctricity Regulatory 
Commission (SERC). The Act requires all consumers t o be metered and also 
mandates supply of electricity through a correct meter. The SERC is required to 
specify an Electricity Supply Code, inter-alia, to provide for recovery of 
electricity charges and intervals for billing of electricity charges. The distribution 
licensee can recover price of electricity from the consumers in accordance with the 
tariff determined by the SERC.

Steps to check power thefts 
510. SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the power utilities in the country still face crippling losses due to 
power thefts which show no sign of abating and whet her such losses work out 
to almost 35 per cent of the power produced; 
(b) whether the Apex Court has, in a recent directive, called for exemplary fines 
and disconnection of power supply for such crimes against the public Utilities; 
and 
(c) what steps are being taken by Government to enforce  the Apex Court's 
directives? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHILKUMAR SHINDE): (a ) 
Government is aware of incidence of theft and pilfe rages in the electricity 
distribution, which indeed is a serious concern for the Govemment. However, since it 
was not possible to exactly assess the amount of th eft in the system, the 
concept of Aggregate. Technical and Commercial (AT& C) losses was 
introduced by the Ministry in 2001-02 to capture total losses, not only technical 
but also commercial including those on account of theft 
210 

[27 November, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
and pilferage, poor metering and billing and non-realisation of dues. AT&C loss 
for 2001-02 of the state power distribution utiliti es at National level was 
38.18%, which came down to 33.82% during 2004-05. 
(b) The Supreme Court while delivering the judgment  in case No. 1113 
of 2006 (Jagmodhan Mehatabsing Gujarat & Others Vs. State of 
Maharashtra) has observed as under: 
"Large scale theft of electricity is a very alarming problem faced by all the 
State Electricity Boards in our country, which is c ausing loss to the Staje 
revenue running in hundreds of crores every year. In our considered view, after 
proper adjudication of the cases of all those who are found to be guilty of the offence 
of committing theft of electricity, apart from the sentence of conviction, the Court 
should invariably impose heavy fine making theft of electricity a wholly non-
profitable venture. The most effective step to curb this tendency perhaps could 
be to discontinue supply of electricity to those co nsumers temporarily or 
permanently who have been caught abstracting electr icity in a cladestine 
manner on more than one occasion. The legislature may consider incorporating 
this suggestion as a form of punishment by amending Section 39 of the Indian 
Electricity Act of 1910." 
(c) The Electricity Act of 1910 was replaced by the  "The Electricity Act, 
2003" which contains provisions for controlling pow er theft. Further, the 
Electricity (Amendment) Bill, 2005 has been introdu ced in the Parliament 
for certain amendments to the Electricity Act, 2003  and there is a proposal 
to bring official amendments to the Bill for provid ing, inter-alia, that all 
offences related to theft of electricity would be c ognizable and non-bailable, 
that the licensee could discorihect supply in case of theft of electricity and 
for debarring large consumer convicted for second t ime from getting supply 
of electricity for a specified period.

the Central Government under section 3 of the Elect ricity Act, 2003 aims at 
accelerated development of power sector, providing electricity supply to all areas and

Government requires the grant of any subsidy to any consumer or class

amount required to compensate the grant of subsidy.  This provision

assisting States in investment in strengthening of sub transmission 
and distribution systems for reducing technical los ses and improving 
the quality of supply and also for incentivising through cash grants for

dealing with theft of electricity.

542. SHRI V. HANUMANTHA RAO: Will the Minister of T RIBAL . 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have received representations to  avoid large 
scale displacement of tribals from any contiguous area; 
(b) if so, whether Government have re-framed its relief  and displacement 
policies; 
 
(c) whether Government have made it mandatory to have t he 
Anthropological Survey of India give its opinon on the social and ethnic 
outcomes of massive displacement from any one homogenous area; 
(d) the specific proposal pending with Government which  involve 
displacement of 5000 or more tribals for any single project; and

THE MINISTER OF TRIBAL AFFAIRS (SHRI P.R. KYNDIAH): (a) Yes, 
Sir. 
(b) Government in the Ministry of Rural Development hav e initiated the 
process of formulating a revised National Rehabilitation Policy-2006 (NRP-2006). 
(c) No, Sir. 
(d) The Polavaram (Indira Sagar) Projects, which involves displacement of 
more than 5000 STs, has been submitted to the Ministry of Tribal Affairs by the 
Government of Andhra Pradesh for clearance of the R esettlement and 
Rehabilitation plan for Scheduled Tribe Project Affected Families (PAFs). The State 
Government has been asked to comply with the required statutory provisions.

Scheduled Areas) Act 1996, policies and the legisla tions of the State 
Government and the National Policy on Resettlement and Rehabilitation of 
Project Affected Families-2003 (NPRR) to protect the interest of project affected

DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that at least 25 per cent of eligible kids, especially 
in the tribal areas of Central India don't get anganwadi project meals and benefits; 
(b) whether Govemment have any special proejct to cover ai! the children, pregnant and 
lactating mothers with this project;

THE MINIS TER OF  S TATE OF  THE M INIS TR Y O F WOMEN AND  CHILD 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI RENUKACHOWDHURY): (a) The Ministry of Women 
and Child Development is administering a Centrally-sponsored Integrated Child 
Development Services (ICDS) Scheme which aims at holistic development of children 
below 6 years of age by providing a package of services comprising supplementary 
nutrition, immunization, health check-up, referral services, pre-school non-formal 
education and nutrition and health education to the children. Pregnant women & lactating 
mothers are also covered under the Scheme. 
Out of 6118 Projects sanctioned so far under the Scheme, 309 are in tribal areas.

pregnant and lactating mothers through a network of about 7.48 lakh operational AWCs 
across the country. As per data of Census 2001, number of children in the age group of 0-6 
is 16.38 crore. Of this, 10.28 crore children are registered at the Anganwadi centres. Thus the 
Scheme covers only 62.76% of children in this age group at present. 
(b) to (d) In pursuance of Government's commitment as enunciated in the National 
Common Minimum Programme and in compliance of the direction of the Supreme 
Court in a PIL fried by the Peoples' Union for Civil Liberties, the ICDS Scheme has been 
expanded to cover 466 additional Projects and 1.88 lakh Anganwadi Centres in 2005-
2006. Of these, 46 Projects and 3353 Anganwadi centres are in tribal areas (excluding

Statement— III  
Steps taken by the Government of NCT of Delhi for tracing the parents of 
inmates and facilitating restoration to their respective families  
A. Steps taken for inmates belonging to Delhi: 
(1) Registered letters/postcards are sent at the address given by children. 
Letters are also sent simultaneously to the in char ges of the local 
police station & Pradhans of the respective villages. Missing Persons 
Squad is also contacted. 
(2) If the parents or the address of children are not traceable then " the 
photographs of such children are published in leading newspapers. 
(3) If the address/the parents are located by the above  two steps, either 
the parents of children turn up to take their child ren or the Welfare 
Office of the institution visit them and facilitates them in restoration 
of their children. 
(4) The last step in restoration in that the parents co me to the Child 
Welfare Committees who after identification handover the children to 
them. 
 
B. Steps taken for inmates belonging to outside Delhi: 
(1) Registered letters/postcards are sent at the addres s given by 
children. Letters are also sent simultaneously to the in charges of the 
local police station & Pradhan of the respective villages. 
(2) Telephonic communication is also made in the cases where the 
children are able to tell their telephone numbers. 
(3) If the address/the parents are located by the above  two, either the 
parents of children turn up to take their children. If the parents are not 
able to come because of poverty or some other reasons, such children 
are sent to their parents or the respective children home of the State 
under Police Protection.

INSTITUTION OF NATIONAL AWARDS FOR OUTSTANDING WORK

THE MINISTER OF SOCIAL JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT 
(SHRIMATI MEIRA KUMAR): Sir, I am glad to inform this august House 
that the Government of India has decided to institute National Awards to 
be given to Non-Govemmental Organisation or Human Rights' activits who 
have done outstanding fieldwork in the area of eradicating untouchability 
and in combating offences of atrocities under the Prevention of Civil Rights 
Act, 1995 and the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of 
Terrorists) Act of 1989. There shall be totally four awards every year covering 
both the categories. Awards to individual activists shall carry an amount of 
Rs. 2 lakhs and to an institution shall carry an amount of Rs. 5 lakhs. The 
wards will be given to outstanding NGOs or Human Rights' activists in

each of the four regions of the country, namely, Norths, South, East and 
West for rendering yeoman service in the said fieids. More than one recipient 
or organisation may share the award. The award will be instituted in 2007, 
and would be given annually thereafter. The award is open to all Indian 
NGOs and Human Rights' activists without any distinction or discrimination 
on ground of race, sex, caste or creed. The Screeni ng Committee and 
finally, the Selection Committee constituted for the purpose would consider 
the achievements of the NGOs or individual Human Ri ghts' activists 
nominated/recommended for Award by the prescribed authority. For the 
2007 Award, the Screening Committee and the Selection Commitee would 
consider nominations received up to 31st January, 2007.

SHORT DURATION DISCUSSION 
On Internal Security Scenario in the Country 
SHRI ARUN JAITLEY (Gujarat): Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, my gratitude 
to you for permitting us to raise the important issue for discussion on the 
internal security situation of the country. Sir, the UPA Government now 
has been in power for almost two-and-a-half years, and during its tenure in 
power, we, in the opposition, have several reasons to be disappointed with 
the performance of this Government. There are several fronts in which the 
Government has certainly not lived up to the popular expectations. We 
have had virtually, because of the ideological struggle between the Congress 
Party and the Left, a paralysis in the economic decision-making process 
of the country. We have seen in the last two-and-a- half years gross 
constitutional improprieties committed for partisan reasons in Jharkhand, 
in Goa, in Bihar; we have seen the dilution of the Prime Ministerial authority; 
we have seen the criminalisation of the Council of Ministers. We have 
seen pronouncements by members of the Council of Ministers, not in the 
direction of any higher standards of governance, but intended to harden 
caste and religious identities of this country. We have also seen the 
abrogation of an effort to pursue an independent foreign policy. Now, if we 
look at the overall performance of the UPA Governme nt, these are the 
broad heads which have disappointed the whole country. But, if there is 
the largest single failure of this Government, it is certainly the management 
of the country's internal security. After two-and-a-half years of the UPA 
being in power, an average citizen is asking himself a question, not merely 
in areas which were traditionally infested with terrorism, but even in other 
parts of the country, that are we really sitting on  a mine field, with the 
helpless Government, unable to have any action or r esponse to the 
developing situation? The question, Sir, is, is India safe in the hands of the 
UPA? And, if we see the performance of this Government, we go back 
285 

RAJYA SABHA [27 November?2006] 
disappointed with a great sense of insecurity that with instance's of terrorism 
and disturbance to internal security increasing by the day, the Government 
is merely a helpless spectator. Every time any major incident of sabotage 
or attack or terrorist violence takes place, we see  the leaders of this 
Government, the hon. Prime Minister, the hon. Home Minister with the 
usual kind of cliches and templates that this is co ndemnable; the 
Government and the country will have zero-tolerance to terrorism. But, 
after these usual templates in terrorism, this Government then sits back 
and waits for the next attack to take place. This has been the history of 
the last two-and-a-half years. Today, we have the situation in Jammu and 
Kashmir, the situation in Assam again erupting, its fall out in various other 
parts of the country, and now you have a complete zone of violence emerging 
from the left wing extremism. If you look at the pr onouncements of the 
Government and even the latest document that they have circulated, you 
will find that there is nothing which inspires real  confidence among the 
people. 
Sir, two-and-a-half years have seen internal security crumbling under 
this Government, if not collapsing. We are disappointed but not surprised. 
I went back to see what is often quoted—National Co mmon Minimum 
Programme—as to what the UPA had to say on the subj ect; because, 
there, when you refer to the National Common Minimum Programme, they 
ask for a strict enforcement. 
As I said, we are disappointed with the internal security situation but 
we are not surprised because the 24-page document virtually made no 
reference to the management of the country's intern al security! The 
management of the internal security in this country is not a UPA priority! 
There is no mention of what the national strategy has to be to deal with 
terrorism, what the way forward has to be in order to ease the situation in 
Jammu and Kashmir, on how the Left Wing extremism has to be combated, 
what is the long-term strategy as far as Jammu and Kashmir is concerned. 
The National Common Minimum Programme of the UPA di d not spare 
much time or attention to all this. It is, therefore, understandable that the 
UPA's approach of inaction to this situation does not bring in turmoil within 
the UPA or its supporting parties in the Left. Because, as we said, we are 
disappointed but not surprised because this certainly not an area of the 
UPA priority. Are the UPA, the hon. Prime Minister, the hon. Home Minister, 
Sir, living in denial about what exactly the situation of the country is? We

do not think that they are really unaware of what is happening. When I say 
they are not unaware, all security and intelligence agencies have a close 
approach to the eyes and ears of the Prime Ministerand the Home Minister. 
And professional as they are, I have no doubt that our agencies have been 
keeping the highest functionaries of the Government informed as to what 
the ground-level situation today in the country is.  We have a situation 
where the Prime Minister and the Home Minister and the entire Government 
pretend to be in denial of this. They are in denial of the existence of this 
problem because virtually it now appears that the crux of the problem is 
not that there is any lack of advisers in the intelligence or security agencies

The point for the Government and the UPA is, Sir, that internal.security

is: Can I make political capital out of it and in fighting terrorism, can I use

Sir, may I end by quoting to you some words of a stirring speech given 
by Kennedy when he was installed as President? I think those words are 
important for countries concerned about their internal security and about 
security in general. Of course, it is the same speech where he also said,

country". In the same speech elsewhere, he said, "Every nation knows 
whether it wishes us well or ill, that we shall pay  any price, bear any 
burden, meet any hardship, support any friend and o ppose any foe, to 
assure the survival and the success of liberty". And the Government of 
India is committed to that. The UPA is committed to that. He also said, 
and that is our approach and that is our philosophy , "If a free society 
cannot help the many who are poor, it cannot save the few who are rich",

fear. But, Sir, we do not fear to negotiate because it is important not to 
negotiate out of fear, but it is equally important not to fear to negotiate.

together. These are matters where the unity of Parliament is more symbolic 
and more important as a message than even the content of what we speak 
here. Let me assure you, as i started by saying that we thank you for this

through you, we are able to convey to the nation what we have done, what 
we are doing and what we are committed to doing. An d the facts and 
figures, in conclusion, I may say, which are availa ble in that book, are

in this country there has been an improvement on co ncrete facts and

I thank you, Sir, very much.
